_comment: Mutations for the Resend transport and the outbox drain. Scored against email_run.sh, a probe pair rather than HTTP cases: the worker has no HTTP surface, and reaching it through the write differential would mean waiting on the very timer the harness pins out of the way everywhere else.

mutations.name: the tick is stamped only after a successful drain
mutations._why: Stamped at the START so an empty outbox still counts as alive. Stamping later makes a healthy worker with nothing to send look wedged to the health probe, which is the one thing that probe exists to distinguish.

mutations.name: stuck sending rows are never reclaimed
mutations._why: A worker that died mid-send leaves the row wedged in `sending` forever, and nothing else in the system moves it.
mutations.new: WHERE status = 'sending' AND last_attempt_at < $1 AND false

mutations.name: the reclaim window is ignored
mutations._why: Sixty seconds gives a send in flight time to finish. Reclaiming immediately would put a row that is mid-send back in the queue and rely entirely on the idempotency key to stop a duplicate.

mutations.name: the batch is not ordered by created_at
mutations._why: Oldest first. Without the order, which mail goes out under a backlog is whatever the planner returns.

mutations.name: the batch size is ignored
mutations._why: The batch bounds how long one tick holds the loop. Draining everything turns a backlog into one very long tick.

mutations.name: rows are not claimed before sending
mutations._why: Flipping the batch to `sending` first is what stops a second worker picking up the same rows, and what the reclaim path keys on.
mutations.old: sqlx::query("UPDATE email_outbox SET status = 'sending', last_attempt_at = $1 WHERE id = ANY($2)")

mutations.name: the suppression list is not consulted
mutations._why: Checked before the API call: it saves a round trip, and re-sending to an address Resend already suppressed is what dings a sender's reputation for every other kind of mail.
mutations.new:
if let Some((reason,)) = None::<(Option<String>,)> {
        let _ = suppressed;

mutations.name: suppression is matched case-sensitively
mutations._why: Addresses are stored lowercased and arrive in whatever case the user typed. A case-sensitive match silently sends to an address that is on the list.

mutations.name: the idempotency key includes the attempt
mutations._why: Every retry of one row must share a key, or the idempotency buys nothing: a retry of an attempt that secretly succeeded delivers a second copy.

mutations.name: a skipped send is treated as a failure
mutations._why: The kill switch being off is not an error. Treating it as one leaves every row retrying until it hits the cap and is marked permanently failed.

mutations.name: a failure past the cap keeps retrying
mutations._why: At the cap the worker stops. Without that, a permanently bad address is retried on every tick forever.

mutations.name: a failure below the cap is terminal
mutations._why: The other direction: one transient Resend 500 would permanently fail a message that a retry would have delivered.

mutations.name: the attempt counter does not advance
mutations._why: It is what the cap is measured against; frozen, the cap is never reached.

mutations.name: a mid-retry failure is logged
mutations._why: The audit trail records outcomes, not attempts: a row that eventually succeeds after two failures should leave one `sent` line, not three.

mutations.name: a sent row keeps its old error
mutations._why: A row that failed and then succeeded must not keep the failure text beside its message id.

mutations.name: the summary counts attempts rather than outcomes
mutations._why: A mid-retry row is in neither bucket: it is counted in the tick it settles in. Counting it as failed double-counts a message that is going to be delivered.

mutations.name: the kill switch is ignored
mutations._why: Defence in depth: a row can reach the outbox while the switch is off, and the transport refuses it rather than trusting the producer to have checked.

mutations.name: an unconfigured transport is retried
mutations._why: A missing key is operator misconfiguration, not an outage — distinct from a 5xx precisely because retrying cannot fix it.

mutations.name: a missing message id is treated as success
mutations._why: Without an id the eventual bounce or complaint webhook cannot be matched back to this row, so the correlation is silently lost.

mutations.name: the SDK's error class is not reproduced
mutations._why: The class name is stored verbatim in two tables. A generic string there loses the distinction between a validation error, a rate limit and an outage — which is what an operator triages on.
mutations.old:
fn sdk_error(code: i64, error_type: &str, message: &str) -> String {
    format!("{}: {message}", resend_error_class(code, error_type))

mutations.name: a successful status with a bad body is not downgraded to 500
mutations._why: The SDK keeps the status when it is 4xx or 5xx and substitutes 500 when it looked successful, which is why a 200 with an empty body is an ApplicationError and a 502 with HTML is a bare ResendError.
mutations.old: let error_code = if status >= 400 { status } else { 500 };

mutations.name: the body's own statusCode is ignored
mutations._why: Resend has answered 200 with an error document. The body's statusCode is consulted precisely for that case.
mutations.old: let effective = if status >= 400 { Some(status) } else { body_status };
mutations.new: let effective = if status >= 400 { Some(status) } else { None };

mutations.name: the content type is not checked
mutations._why: A CDN or proxy answering HTML is not a Resend error document, and parsing it as one would report whatever JSON fragment happened to be inside.

mutations.name: the idempotency key is sent as a message header
mutations._why: It has to be an HTTP header to Resend. As a message header it becomes an SMTP header on the outgoing mail and Resend delivers a fresh copy on every retry — silently, which is what makes it worth a mutation.
